messages.content: A consistent-hash ring has only one token per node and shows severe load imbalance with 64 nodes. Analyze the use of virtual nodes/tokens.

With few random positions, key ranges can vary widely in size and create uneven load. Giving each physical node multiple well-distributed virtual positions usually smooths the distribution and makes incremental membership changes move smaller ranges. Measure keys/bytes/QPS per node before and after changing token count. Too many virtual nodes increase metadata/rebalancing complexity, so choose enough to meet balance goals rather than maximizing the count.

verification.details: Must connect sparse token placement to imbalance, explain how multiple virtual positions smooth ranges, and require measured balance versus metadata/rebalance cost.

messages.content: A kernel streams over a large output buffer, writing each cache line once and never reading it soon afterward. Analyze whether ordinary write-allocate traffic is wasting bandwidth.

On write-allocate caches, a store miss can trigger a read-for-ownership of the cache line before it is modified, adding memory traffic even when the old contents are irrelevant. Measure memory-controller traffic and compare with non-temporal/streaming stores where the ISA and alignment/workload make them appropriate. Streaming stores can reduce cache pollution and read-for-ownership traffic, but they have ordering/alignment rules and are poor when the data will be reused soon.

verification.details: Must explain read-for-ownership/write-allocate traffic, compare with measured non-temporal stores, and state reuse/order tradeoffs.

messages.content: Production investigation: A zero-copy pipeline uses `splice()` through a pipe between two file descriptors. Throughput stalls whenever the downstream side slows. Analyze the role of pipe capacity and backpressure.

`splice()` can avoid copying through userspace, but data still flows through finite kernel pipe buffers. If the downstream destination cannot drain, the pipe fills and upstream splice calls block or return `EAGAIN` in nonblocking mode. Measure pipe/readiness behavior, downstream throughput, and syscall timing. Use bounded event-driven flow control and avoid assuming zero-copy means infinite buffering or no backpressure. Increasing pipe capacity may smooth bursts but does not fix a sustained downstream bottleneck.

verification.details: Must connect stalls to finite pipe capacity/downstream drain rate, preserve bounded backpressure, and reject the idea that zero-copy removes queueing limits.

messages.content: Production investigation: A workload spends 5% of runtime in code that cannot be parallelized. Estimate the theoretical maximum speedup with unlimited processors and explain what the bound means.

Amdahl's Law gives maximum speedup `1 / f_serial`. With a serial fraction of 5%, `f_serial = 5/100`, so the unlimited-processor upper bound is `100/5`×. This is a model bound, not a performance promise: synchronization, memory bandwidth, scheduling, and load imbalance can reduce real speedup further. The exercise is useful for deciding whether optimizing the serial portion may matter more than adding processors.

verification.details: Must compute the unlimited-processor bound as 100/5, identify the serial fraction, and state that real systems can be slower due to additional overheads.

messages.content: A latency-sensitive database shares an SSD with background sequential writes. Analyze whether block I/O scheduling/queueing is hurting tail latency.

Measure device latency distribution, queue depth, per-cgroup/process I/O, throughput, and scheduler policy under mixed load. Compare controlled runs with background traffic limited or isolated and, where appropriate, alternative scheduler/cgroup I/O policies. The right policy depends on the device and workload: modern NVMe behavior differs from rotational disks. The goal is to bound interference, not to pick a scheduler by name without evidence.

verification.details: Must use latency/queue/per-workload I/O evidence, test isolation or policy changes, and avoid universal scheduler claims.

messages.content: A controlled network supports ECN end-to-end. Analyze how ECN can signal congestion before packet loss and how to verify it is actually negotiated.

ECN-capable endpoints can mark packets/echo congestion information instead of relying only on drops, allowing congestion control to reduce sending rate while avoiding some loss/retransmission cost. Verify negotiation in the handshake/protocol state and capture CE/ECE/CWR-style signals or stack counters as appropriate. Compare queue delay, retransmissions, and throughput with and without ECN under the same bottleneck. ECN does not create capacity; it changes congestion signalling behavior and depends on compatible endpoints/network devices.

verification.details: Must require end-to-end negotiation/counter evidence, compare congestion behavior, and state that ECN signals rather than removes congestion.

messages.content: A mechanical button generates many GPIO transitions for one press. Implement a debounce policy without blocking the whole firmware for 50 ms.

On an edge, record the time/state and start or reset a debounce timer/state machine. Accept a new stable logical state only after the input has remained consistently at that level for the debounce interval; then emit one event. Continue servicing other firmware work while waiting. For interrupt-driven GPIO, keep the ISR minimal and perform the timed validation outside it. The exact interval should come from switch characteristics and UX requirements rather than an arbitrary long busy-wait.

verification.details: Must avoid blocking delay loops, require a timed stable-state check, keep ISR work minimal, and produce one logical event per physical transition.

messages.content: A consensus follower is so far behind that the leader has compacted the log entries it needs. Implement the recovery path using a snapshot.

The leader transfers a complete snapshot representing state through a specific committed index/term. The follower writes it to temporary durable state, validates completeness/integrity, atomically installs it, discards log prefixes covered by the snapshot, then resumes replication from the snapshot boundary. Interrupted transfers must not replace the current state with a partial snapshot, and stale snapshots must not roll state backward. Membership/configuration state included in the snapshot must follow the protocol's rules.

verification.details: Must install only a complete validated snapshot, preserve atomic recovery after interruption, align log state to the snapshot index/term, and reject stale rollback.

messages.content: Production investigation: A search service writes 1000 rows one transaction at a time and spends most of its time in transaction/round-trip overhead. Analyze bounded bulk-write chunking.

Measure per-transaction latency, server round trips, log/fsync behavior, lock duration, and throughput. Grouping rows into bounded transactions amortizes fixed commit and network cost, but extremely large transactions increase lock hold time, rollback work, replication lag, and memory pressure. Sweep chunk size and choose the knee that improves throughput while keeping latency and failure recovery acceptable. Preserve idempotency or retry semantics for a partially completed multi-chunk job.

verification.details: Must identify fixed transaction/round-trip overhead, explain why batching helps, include costs of oversized transactions, and require measured chunk-size selection.

messages.content: Production investigation: A loop walks a large array with stride 8 cache lines. Sequential access is fast, but this pattern loses bandwidth. Analyze hardware-prefetch effectiveness.

Hardware prefetchers recognize only certain spatial/stride patterns and have finite lookahead/resources. Measure cache misses, memory bandwidth, and prefetch-related counters if available while varying stride. Compare with sequential access and an explicit blocking/reordering strategy. A large or irregular stride can defeat prefetch and waste most bytes fetched per cache line. Software prefetch is only justified after measurement because it can increase bandwidth pressure or pollution.

verification.details: Must vary stride with cache/memory evidence, explain prefetch-pattern limits, and avoid assuming software prefetch is automatically beneficial.

messages.content: A privileged tool must construct a new file privately and expose it by name only after all contents and metadata are valid. Design a Linux approach using an unnamed temporary inode when available.

Create the file with `O_TMPFILE` in the target filesystem/directory, write and validate contents, set required metadata, and flush according to durability requirements. Only after the object is complete should it be linked into the namespace using the supported descriptor-relative mechanism. This avoids a partially initialized temporary pathname visible to other processes. Provide a safe fallback for filesystems without `O_TMPFILE`, and still handle directory durability when crash consistency matters.

verification.details: Must keep the object unnamed during construction, publish only after validation, stay on the target filesystem, and include a safe fallback/durability discussion.

messages.content: A browser application authenticates with cookies. Design CSRF protection without assuming `SameSite` alone is sufficient for every deployment.

Use the appropriate `SameSite` cookie setting as one layer, but protect state-changing requests with an anti-CSRF token or a same-origin/custom-header pattern appropriate to the architecture, and validate Origin/Referer where reliable as defense in depth. Avoid state changes via GET. Account for cross-site login/payment flows that may require less restrictive cookie behavior. CSRF protection addresses ambient cookie authority; it does not replace XSS prevention, which can often bypass in-page token defenses.

verification.details: Must include an explicit anti-CSRF mechanism for state changes, treat SameSite as layered protection, avoid unsafe GET semantics, and distinguish CSRF from XSS.

messages.content: A cache-sensitive worker migrates frequently among CPUs and shows unstable latency. Analyze whether tighter affinity could help without assuming pinning is always better.

Measure CPU migrations, cache/TLB miss behavior, run-queue pressure, NUMA locality, and latency. Pinning or a smaller affinity mask can improve locality when the worker repeatedly loses warm cache state, but it can hurt load balancing and create hotspots when chosen CPUs become busy. Compare unrestricted scheduling with topology-aware affinity under the same workload. The decision should balance locality against scheduler flexibility rather than treating migration count alone as a bug.

verification.details: Must measure migrations/locality and run-queue effects, test controlled affinity, and state the load-balancing tradeoff.

messages.content: Distributed training waits for one very large gradient all-reduce near the end of backward. Analyze gradient bucket sizing for communication overlap.

Smaller buckets can launch all-reduces as groups of gradients become ready, overlapping communication with later backward compute. Buckets that are too small increase collective launch/protocol overhead, while buckets that are too large delay communication until late in the step. Use a timeline to measure ready times, collective duration, overlap, and step time across bucket sizes. Choose the knee for the actual topology/model.

verification.details: Must explain overlap versus launch-overhead tradeoff, use timeline evidence, and tune from measured step time/topology.

messages.content: Implementation review: A thread-safe map is used for memoization in a API gateway, but the code does `if key not in map: map[key] = compute()` and expensive computation still runs multiple times concurrently. Repair the pattern.

A thread-safe container makes individual operations safe but does not make the compound check-then-compute sequence atomic. Use a per-key once/future/promise entry, a compute-if-absent primitive whose semantics guarantee the needed behavior, or a per-key lock. Avoid one global lock around all computations. Define failure behavior so a failed computation does not leave a permanently poisoned entry unless that is intentional.

verification.details: Must identify the compound-operation race, coalesce computation per key, avoid global serialization, and define cleanup after failed computation.

messages.content: A multi-threaded event loop uses `EPOLLONESHOT`. After one readiness event is handled, some sockets are never reported again. Repair the lifecycle.

`EPOLLONESHOT` disables further notifications for that file descriptor after an event is delivered. After draining/processing the current readiness according to the nonblocking protocol, explicitly rearm the descriptor with `epoll_ctl(..., EPOLL_CTL_MOD, ...)`. Coordinate ownership so only the intended worker rearms it, and handle close/error races. If edge-triggered semantics are also used, drain until `EAGAIN` before rearming to avoid leaving unread work stranded.

verification.details: Must identify missing EPOLLONESHOT rearm, require explicit MOD rearm, and address nonblocking drain plus ownership/close races.

messages.content: A 4096 MiB random-access working set has a high TLB-miss rate even though cache behavior is acceptable. Analyze TLB reach and page size.

TLB reach is approximately the number of usable translations times page size, so a large randomly accessed working set can exceed it and repeatedly walk page tables. Measure TLB miss/page-walk counters and compare normal pages with an appropriate huge-page configuration while holding the algorithm constant. Larger pages can reduce translation pressure but increase fragmentation, allocation constraints, and memory waste. Improvement in page-walk cost with stable cache behavior supports the diagnosis.

verification.details: Must connect working-set size to TLB reach, use page-walk/TLB evidence, and state huge-page tradeoffs.

messages.content: Implementation review: Implement a token-bucket limiter for a API gateway allowing an average of 500 requests/s with a short burst of 100 requests.

Maintain a bucket with capacity 100. Refill tokens as a function of elapsed monotonic time at 500 tokens/s up to the capacity. Each admitted request consumes one token; when none are available, reject, queue within a bounded deadline, or return retry guidance according to API policy. Synchronize updates so concurrent callers cannot overspend the bucket. Use monotonic time so wall-clock adjustments do not create artificial refill. The burst capacity controls short spikes; the refill rate controls the long-run average.

verification.details: Must use monotonic elapsed-time refill, cap the bucket at 100, prevent concurrent overspend, and distinguish burst capacity from sustained rate 500/s.

ECN-capable endpoints can mark packets/echo congestion information instead of relying only on drops, allowing congestion control to reduce sending rate while avoiding some loss/retransmission cost. Verify negotiation in the handshake/protocol state and capture CE/ECE/CWR-style signals or stack counters as appropriate. Compare queue delay, retransmissions, and throughput with and without ECN under the same bottleneck. ECN does not create capacity; it changes congestion signalling behavior and depends on compatible endpoints/network devices.

verification.details: Must require end-to-end negotiation/counter evidence, compare congestion behavior, and state that ECN signals rather than removes congestion.

messages.content: A device writes a small status record every 60 seconds to the same flash page. Design storage so the page does not wear out prematurely.

Flash has finite erase/program endurance and often erases in blocks larger than one record. Use a log-structured or rotating set of slots/pages, append new records with sequence/version and integrity metadata, and erase/recycle only after consuming available slots. Batch or reduce writes when semantics permit. Recovery should choose the newest valid record after power loss. Estimate lifetime from write frequency, erase-block endurance, and wear distribution rather than assuming nominal flash capacity implies unlimited updates.

verification.details: Must distribute writes/erases, include power-loss-safe version/integrity recovery, and reason from write frequency/endurance.

messages.content: A timeout is computed from wall-clock time. When the administrator steps the clock backward, an operation waits far longer than intended. Repair the clock choice.

Use a monotonic clock for measuring elapsed durations and deadlines that should not track civil-time adjustments. Capture a monotonic start/deadline and compare using that same clock domain. Keep wall time for timestamps presented to humans or calendar events. If suspend time must count toward the timeout, choose a monotonic/boottime clock with the required suspend semantics. Mixing clock domains in one deadline calculation is also a bug.

verification.details: Must replace wall-clock elapsed-time logic with an appropriate monotonic clock and state suspend/clock-domain semantics.

messages.content: A server uses `sendfile()` once to transmit a 1024 MiB file and assumes the whole file was sent whenever the call returns a positive number. Repair the transfer loop.

Treat the positive return as progress, not completion. Advance the offset and remaining byte count and continue until the requested range is fully sent. Handle `EINTR` by retrying, and handle `EAGAIN`/`EWOULDBLOCK` through the nonblocking readiness path. A zero return before the expected range completes needs policy appropriate to the file/source state. The loop must also respect platform limits on one-call transfer size.

verification.details: Must loop on partial positive results, preserve offset/progress, handle EINTR and nonblocking readiness, and not equate one successful call with full transfer.

messages.content: Architecture review: A service has an RPO of 5 minutes and an RTO of 5 minutes. Explain how those two targets constrain backup/replication and recovery design.

RPO bounds acceptable data loss, so the system needs replication/checkpoint/backup frequency and durability capable of losing no more than about 5 minutes of committed state under the defined disaster. RTO bounds how long service restoration may take, so restore automation, data volume, validation, failover capacity, and operator procedures must fit within 5 minutes. A backup schedule can satisfy RPO yet still miss RTO if restoration is too slow. Test both with recovery exercises rather than inferring them from backup existence.

verification.details: Must distinguish data-loss objective (RPO 5 min) from restoration-time objective (RTO 5 min) and require tested recovery.

messages.content: Implementation review: A billing service starts 64 child tasks for one request. If one child fails or the client disconnects, the remaining tasks currently continue running in the background. Implement a structured-concurrency policy.

Tie child task lifetime to the parent request scope. Create children under a task group/scope that propagates cancellation and joins them before the scope exits. If policy is fail-fast, the first substantive child failure cancels siblings; if partial success is allowed, encode that explicitly rather than leaking work. Ensure cleanup runs on cancellation and that shared resources are released exactly once. Detached background tasks should be used only when their lifetime is intentionally independent of the request.

verification.details: Must bind child lifetime to parent scope, propagate cancellation, join/clean up children, and distinguish intentional detached work from accidental task leakage.

messages.content: A process temporarily stores a cryptographic secret in memory. Decide when explicit zeroization is useful and why a normal `memset` may not be sufficient.

Zeroization can reduce the lifetime of secrets in process memory and crash/core artifacts after the value is no longer needed. Compilers may remove an ordinary `memset` that has no observable effect, so use a platform/library primitive intended not to be optimized away. Minimize copies and lifetime in the first place. Zeroization is defense in depth: it cannot erase copies made elsewhere, registers, swap, prior dumps, or an attacker that already read the secret.

verification.details: Must explain dead-store optimization risk, require a dedicated zeroization primitive, minimize copies/lifetime, and state the limits of zeroization.

messages.content: A host shows only 55% average CPU use, yet latency is poor. Decide how Linux Pressure Stall Information can add evidence beyond utilization.

Utilization says how busy resources are but not how much time runnable work is stalled waiting for CPU, memory reclaim, or I/O. PSI reports time some/all tasks are delayed by resource pressure. Correlate CPU/memory/I/O PSI with service latency and cgroup-level metrics. High PSI with moderate average utilization can reveal concentrated contention or reclaim/IO stalls. PSI is a signal for investigation/capacity control, not a diagnosis by itself.

verification.details: Must distinguish utilization from stall time, correlate PSI dimensions with latency/cgroup evidence, and avoid treating PSI alone as root-cause proof.

messages.content: Architecture review: A public TCP service experiences bursts that fill the SYN backlog. Decide when SYN cookies are an appropriate protection and what they do not solve.

SYN cookies can allow the server to avoid retaining normal per-half-open-connection state when the SYN queue is under pressure, helping resist state exhaustion. They do not provide unlimited application capacity, do not stop established-connection resource exhaustion, and can constrain TCP option negotiation depending on implementation. Confirm backlog drops/SYN pressure first, keep normal backlog sizing and admission controls, and use cookies as one layer of protection rather than a substitute for DDoS filtering or capacity planning.

verification.details: Must explain half-open state protection, state limits of SYN cookies, require backlog-pressure evidence, and avoid presenting them as general DDoS/capacity protection.

messages.content: A crashing service restarts hundreds of times per minute and floods logs. Configure systemd so restart remains automatic but runaway restart loops are bounded.

Keep the desired `Restart=` policy, then configure unit start-rate limiting (`StartLimitIntervalSec=`/`StartLimitBurst=` or the version-appropriate equivalent) so repeated failures eventually stop automatic starts for the interval. Use `RestartSec=` to add delay between attempts. Pick values from recovery objectives, not arbitrary numbers, and alert when the limit is hit. Rate limiting prevents a tight restart loop; it does not fix the underlying crash.

verification.details: Must combine restart policy with bounded start-rate limiting and retry delay, explain the operational tradeoff, and require alerting/root-cause work.

messages.content: A failed primary becomes partitioned, a new primary is elected, and the old primary later resumes issuing writes to shared storage. Design a fencing mechanism.

Assign each ownership grant a strictly increasing fencing token/epoch. Every write to the protected resource carries that token, and the storage/resource layer records the highest token seen and rejects operations from lower, stale epochs. Revoking a lease or electing a new primary is not enough if the old process can still reach the resource. Fencing moves stale-owner rejection to the place where conflicting effects occur.

verification.details: Must use monotonically increasing ownership tokens enforced by the protected resource and explain why election/lease state alone cannot stop a stale process.

messages.content: Production investigation: A client keeps connecting to an old service address minutes after DNS has changed. The authoritative record is correct. Diagnose TTL and local caching behavior.

Inspect the record TTL, recursive resolver cache, OS/runtime/application DNS caches, and whether the client library pins resolved addresses longer than DNS semantics intend. Query each layer separately to locate stale state. A low authoritative TTL cannot force a runtime that caches forever to refresh correctly, while setting TTL near zero increases resolver load and may still be bounded by cache minimums. Fix the layer violating the desired refresh policy.

verification.details: Must inspect authoritative TTL plus resolver/OS/runtime caches, locate the stale layer, and avoid assuming authoritative DNS changes instantly reach clients.

messages.content: Architecture review: A GPU graph executes several tiny elementwise kernels that each read and rewrite the same tensor. Design a fusion test.

Fuse compatible operations so intermediate values stay in registers/on-chip state where possible and the tensor is read/written fewer times. Compare kernel count, global-memory bytes, occupancy/register pressure, and end-to-end latency. Fusion helps when launch and memory traffic dominate, but an overly large fused kernel can increase register pressure and reduce occupancy. Keep numerical semantics and synchronization dependencies unchanged.

verification.details: Must compare memory traffic/kernel count before and after fusion, include register/occupancy tradeoffs, and preserve numerical/dependency semantics.

messages.content: Implementation review: A server uses `sendfile()` once to transmit a 256 MiB file and assumes the whole file was sent whenever the call returns a positive number. Repair the transfer loop.

Handle `EINTR` by retrying, and handle `EAGAIN`/`EWOULDBLOCK` through the nonblocking readiness path. A zero return before the expected range completes needs policy appropriate to the file/source state. The loop must also respect platform limits on one-call transfer size.

verification.details: Must loop on partial positive results, preserve offset/progress, handle EINTR and nonblocking readiness, and not equate one successful call with full transfer.

messages.content: An ADC samples a periodic signal at 16 kHz and reports a much lower apparent frequency that changes when the sample rate is adjusted. Explain aliasing.

Sampling cannot uniquely represent frequency content above the Nyquist limit without prior filtering. Components above half the sample rate can fold into lower apparent frequencies. Confirm by changing sample rate and observing the predicted alias movement, and inspect the analog spectrum. Use an anti-alias filter and a sample rate with sufficient margin for the signal bandwidth. Digital post-processing after aliased sampling cannot reconstruct information that was never captured unambiguously.

verification.details: Must explain Nyquist/alias folding, require sample-rate/spectrum evidence, and recommend adequate sampling plus analog anti-alias filtering.

messages.content: Architecture review: Two compute configurations complete the same job: A uses 120 W for 20 minutes, while B uses 160 W for 35 minutes. Explain how to compare energy efficiency instead of power alone.

Energy is power multiplied by time. Configuration A uses approximately `120 W × 20/60 h`; B uses `160 W × 35/60 h`. Compare watt-hours (or joules) for the completed job, then separately consider latency, thermal limits, electricity price, and hardware constraints. Lower instantaneous power does not guarantee lower total energy if the job runs much longer, and the lowest-energy choice may still be unacceptable if it misses a latency/SLA target.

verification.details: Must compare power×time energy for the same completed work and distinguish energy efficiency from instantaneous power and latency requirements.

Each admitted request consumes one token; when none are available, reject, queue within a bounded deadline, or return retry guidance according to API policy. Synchronize updates so concurrent callers cannot overspend the bucket. Use monotonic time so wall-clock adjustments do not create artificial refill. The burst capacity controls short spikes; the refill rate controls the long-run average.

verification.details: Must use monotonic elapsed-time refill, cap the bucket at 20, prevent concurrent overspend, and distinguish burst capacity from sustained rate 100/s.

Hardware prefetchers recognize only certain spatial/stride patterns and have finite lookahead/resources. Measure cache misses, memory bandwidth, and prefetch-related counters if available while varying stride. Compare with sequential access and an explicit blocking/reordering strategy. A large or irregular stride can defeat prefetch and waste most bytes fetched per cache line. Software prefetch is only justified after measurement because it can increase bandwidth pressure or pollution.

verification.details: Must vary stride with cache/memory evidence, explain prefetch-pattern limits, and avoid assuming software prefetch is automatically beneficial.

messages.content: Production investigation: A service writes large temporary files to tmpfs. Disk usage looks fine, but the host develops memory pressure and swap activity. Explain why.

tmpfs stores file contents in memory (and can use swap), so growth consumes the same broad memory resources that applications/page cache rely on rather than ordinary disk blocks. Measure tmpfs usage, resident/swap pressure, cgroup memory accounting, and the writer's lifecycle. Set explicit size/cgroup limits and clean up files. Treating tmpfs as 'free fast disk' can move a storage-capacity problem into memory pressure.

verification.details: Must connect tmpfs growth to memory/swap accounting, require usage/pressure evidence, and recommend bounded limits/cleanup.

messages.content: A replicated store sometimes reads divergent versions from replicas. Decide when read repair is useful and why it cannot be the only repair mechanism.

A read can compare replica versions, return the value chosen by the consistency/conflict rule, and asynchronously update stale replicas. This opportunistically repairs keys that are actually read. Cold keys may remain inconsistent indefinitely, so background anti-entropy/repair is still needed for complete convergence. Measure repair volume and read latency, and ensure version metadata makes stale versus newer data unambiguous.

verification.details: Must explain opportunistic repair on reads, identify the cold-key limitation, require version/conflict semantics, and retain background repair.

messages.content: Production investigation: Two messages are encrypted under the same AEAD key and accidentally reuse the same nonce. Explain why this can be catastrophic even though authentication tags are present.

Many AEAD constructions require nonce uniqueness per key. Reuse can reveal relationships between plaintexts and, for some modes, enable authentication forgeries by exposing algebraic structure. The exact failure depends on the algorithm, but the API contract must treat nonce uniqueness as a hard invariant unless the construction explicitly provides misuse resistance. Generate nonces with a scheme that guarantees uniqueness for the key lifecycle, rotate keys safely, and do not rely on random chance when the message volume makes collisions meaningful.

verification.details: Must state nonce uniqueness as an AEAD requirement, explain confidentiality/authentication risk, and require a deterministic or otherwise robust uniqueness strategy.
